When "regenerate" is used as an adjective, it describes a person (or sometimes a thing) that has been renewed, reformed, or spiritually reborn — someone who was once corrupt, sinful, or morally lost, but has since undergone a deep inner transformation and is now in a better, purer state.

Think of it this way: the person existed in a "fallen" or degraded condition, and then something changed them at a fundamental level, bringing them into a new, improved state of being.

The adjective "regenerate" carries the idea of complete internal change, not just surface-level improvement. It is not about someone who merely behaved better for a week, or who cleaned up their habits slightly. It points to something far deeper — a person whose very character, soul, or inner nature has been genuinely transformed.

This word is most at home in religious and theological contexts, where it describes a soul that has been spiritually reborn through divine grace. In Christian theology especially, a "regenerate" soul is one that has received new spiritual life — a person who was spiritually dead or corrupt is now spiritually alive and renewed. This is closely connected to the concept of being "born again."

But the word is not confined only to religion. In a broader sense, it can describe anyone who has gone from a corrupt, degenerate, or morally broken state to one of genuine reform and goodness.

To fully understand "regenerate," it helps enormously to understand its opposite: unregenerate.

An unregenerate person is one who is stubbornly, obstinately stuck in their corrupt ways — someone who has not been reformed, has not repented, and shows no sign of inner change. They resist renewal.

A regenerate person, by contrast, has crossed over. The transformation has already happened. They are on the other side of that change.

So when you call someone "regenerate," you are saying: this person has been fundamentally changed for the better — they have been renewed from within.
Nuance: It Describes a State, Not an Action

This is a subtle but important point. As an adjective, "regenerate" describes the condition someone is already in, not what they are doing. It says: the renewal has occurred; this person now exists in a regenerated state.

Compare this to the verb form, which describes the act of regenerating something. The adjective simply labels the result — the person or thing is regenerate. It is a descriptor of their current status.

• "After years of violence and crime, he emerged from prison a truly regenerate man — calm, compassionate, and committed to making amends."
  • "The preacher gave thanks for every regenerate soul in his congregation."
  • "She was no longer the selfish, bitter woman she had once been; she was, in every sense, regenerate."
  • "The philosophy sought to build a regenerate society from the ruins of the corrupt one."

In each of these, the word signals that a profound, real transformation has taken place — not a pretense, but a genuine renewal.
The Weight and Register of This Word

"Regenerate" as an adjective is a formal and somewhat elevated word. You will encounter it most in theological writing, literature, moral philosophy, and serious prose. It is rarely used in casual conversation. When a writer chooses this word, they are deliberately signalling depth — a true, internal, lasting change rather than a superficial one.

It carries a note of hope and affirmation. To call someone "regenerate" is to affirm that real change is possible, and that this particular person has achieved it.

The adjective "regenerate" means: having been spiritually, morally, or fundamentally renewed and transformed from a corrupt or fallen state into a better one. It points to deep, genuine, internal change — the kind that reshapes a person's very nature, not just their outward behavior. It is most common in religious contexts but extends to any domain where profound inner reform is the subject.
